passage: The Mughal administration was a complex system designed to manage a vast territory. Officers known as mansabdars held a 'zat' rank, which determined their personal status and salary, rather than the number of animals they owned. These officers were assigned 'jagirs', which were revenue-collecting areas, but they did not own the land; they could only collect taxes, and they were frequently transferred to prevent them from becoming too powerful. Revenue collection was primarily managed through the 'zabt' system, which involved careful surveys of crop yields and prices, though this system could not be applied in areas like Gujarat or Bengal where local conditions differed. While the Emperor appointed many officials, local hereditary landlords called zamindars often acted as intermediaries to collect revenue from peasants. Regarding their heritage, the Mughals were proud of their Timurid ancestry and disliked being called Mongols, as the Mongol name was associated with the massacre of countless people. Furthermore, Akbar’s policy of 'sulh-i kul' or 'universal peace' was not a new religion, but a philosophy of tolerance that allowed people of different faiths to coexist peacefully in his empire.

items.evidence: Officers known as mansabdars held a 'zat' rank, which determined their personal status and salary, rather than the number of animals they owned.
items.q: A mansabdar's zat rank is raised. What most likely changes for him?
options: His personal status and salary go up
His herd of animals grows larger
His revenue area becomes his own land
items.explain: Zat rank decided an officer's personal status and salary, not the animals he owned.

wrong.why: thinks zat rank counts animals owned
thinks jagirs become permanent land gifts
thinks higher rank means staying in one place

items.evidence: These officers were assigned 'jagirs', which were revenue-collecting areas, but they did not own the land; they could only collect taxes, and they were frequently transferred to prevent them from becoming too powerful.
items.q: Why were mansabdars often moved from one jagir to another?
options: So no officer gained too much power
So each officer could own more land
So every area paid the same tax
So officers could rule like local kings
items.explain: They only collected taxes and were transferred often so that none became too powerful.

wrong.why: thinks jagirs were land officers could own
thinks transfers were about one tax system

items.evidence: While the Emperor appointed many officials, local hereditary landlords called zamindars often acted as intermediaries to collect revenue from peasants.
items.q: How was a zamindar different from an officer sent by the Emperor?
options: He was a local landlord by inheritance
He was an official posted from Delhi
He was a mansabdar with a high zat
He was a ruler of a Rajput kingdom
items.explain: Zamindars were local hereditary landlords who collected revenue, not officials the Emperor appointed.

wrong.why: thinks zamindars were officials appointed from Delhi

items.evidence: Furthermore, Akbar’s policy of 'sulh-i kul' or 'universal peace' was not a new religion, but a philosophy of tolerance that allowed people of different faiths to coexist peacefully in his empire.
items.q: A subject follows a different faith from Akbar. What does sulh-i kul mean for him?
options: He can live in peace with others
He must join a faith Akbar created
He must pay a special tax for peace
He must follow the zabt rules
items.explain: Sulh-i kul was a philosophy of tolerance letting people of different faiths live together peacefully.

wrong.why: thinks sulh-i kul was a new forced religion
thinks peace was bought through a tax
mixes the policy up with the zabt system
